title: Review an HTTP client implementation that creates sockets repeatedly
description: Problem: Review an HTTP client implementation that creates sockets repeatedly. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: An API creates a new HttpClient instance for every outgoing request instead of reusing a single instance. Each HttpClient creates a new socket connection, performs the request, and disposes the socket. Under moderate load, the application exhausts the available socket ports, triggers port exhaustion errors, and begins failing with SocketException. The problem is intermittent in development and guaranteed in production.

items: Understand why HttpClient is designed to be instantiated once and reused for the application lifetime
Learn how socket exhaustion occurs when connections are not pooled
Identify the difference between HttpClient, HttpClientFactory, and SocketsHttpHandler
Apply dependency injection and IHttpClientFactory to manage HTTP client lifetimes correctly

terms.definition: A condition where the operating system runs out of available TCP ports because connections are opened and closed faster than they enter TIME_WAIT state.
An ASP.NET Core service that manages HttpClient lifetimes, pooling, and DNS refresh automatically.
The default HTTP handler in .NET Core that manages connection pooling, DNS, and HTTP/2.
A TCP state where a closed socket remains reserved for a period to ensure delayed packets are discarded.

data.text: Creating HttpClient per request is one of the most common and most damaging performance mistakes in .NET. It exhausts sockets, causes DNS resolution to fail because connections are cached indefinitely, and triggers cascading failures when the application cannot reach any external service. The fix is simple: register HttpClient once and let the framework manage it.

data.title: New HttpClient per request is an anti-pattern
data.text: Microsoft explicitly documents that HttpClient should be instantiated once and reused. Creating it per request causes socket exhaustion, DNS problems, and unpredictable behavior under load.

The problematic code creates a new HttpClient inside a method or controller action. Each instance creates a new socket, sends the request, and leaves the socket in TIME_WAIT. After a few hundred requests, the application cannot open new connections and begins throwing SocketException. The developer may not notice in local testing because the request volume is low.

data.text: The correct implementation uses IHttpClientFactory, registered in Program.cs, to create and manage HttpClient instances. The factory pools connections, handles DNS refresh, and integrates with Polly for resilience. Each named or typed client gets its own configuration, and the factory ensures the underlying SocketsHttpHandler is reused.

data.title: Symptoms and tools
items: Error messages: 'No such host is known' or 'An attempt was made to access a socket in a way forbidden by its access permissions'
netstat -ano shows thousands of connections in TIME_WAIT state
Performance counters show low available ports and high connection rate
Event log entries for HTTP.sys or socket errors under load

data.title: DNS and stale connections
data.text: A static HttpClient also caches DNS for the lifetime of the handler. If the downstream service changes its IP address, the client continues hitting the old address. IHttpClientFactory periodically refreshes DNS by creating new handlers.

items.question: Is HttpClient disposable?
items.answer: Yes, but you should not dispose it after every use. When you use IHttpClientFactory, the factory manages the lifetime and disposal of the underlying handler. Your typed client should not dispose the injected HttpClient.

items.question: What is the default connection limit in .NET?
items.answer: ServicePointManager.DefaultConnectionLimit is often 2 per host in .NET Framework. In .NET Core, SocketsHttpHandler defaults to int.MaxValue, but per-request creation still causes socket exhaustion through TIME_WAIT accumulation.

items.question: Can I reuse HttpClient across services?
items.answer: Yes, but prefer typed clients for testability and configuration. Each typed client gets its own named HttpClient with its own configuration while sharing the underlying handler pool.

items.question: What about gRPC clients?
items.answer: gRPC clients are also designed to be reused. Use AddGrpcClient with IHttpClientFactory for the same connection pooling and resilience benefits.

data.title: Fix socket exhaustion
data.description: Refactor an application that creates HttpClient per request to use IHttpClientFactory.
steps: Search the codebase for new HttpClient() inside methods
Define a typed client interface and implementation for each external API
Register typed clients in Program.cs using AddHttpClient
Inject the typed client instead of creating HttpClient inline
Run a load test and verify socket counts stay stable
data.expectedOutcome: The application reuses connections through a pooled handler. Socket counts remain stable under load, and DNS changes are picked up automatically.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: HttpClient is intended to be reused for the lifetime of the application
IHttpClientFactory manages pooling, DNS, and Polly integration
Socket exhaustion manifests as intermittent failures under load
Typed clients make dependency injection and testing straightforward
data.takeaway: A new HttpClient per request is not a harmless shortcut; it is a production incident in waiting.
